title: Our African Origin and the Humans We Met

scenes.tts: Our species, Homo sapiens, arose in Africa. Not in one place, and not at one moment. People with partly modern anatomy lived in north Africa about three hundred thousand years ago, and in east Africa by at least two hundred thirty-three thousand years ago, in populations that split and merged again. Later, some of their descendants spread across the world, met Neanderthals and Denisovans, and had children with them. Pieces of that D N A survive in people today.

scenes.visual: Map of Africa with two glowing points, north (Jebel Irhoud, about 300,000) and east (Omo, at least 233,000), joined by shifting, branching and re-merging threads; threads then stream out of Africa across Eurasia, meet two other colored threads (Neanderthal, Denisovan) and braid briefly; end on a present-day chromosome bar with a few small archaic-colored pieces.

scenes.tts: Fossil dates need care. At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, flints heated by fire lay with the bones, and they give the date. The face looks like ours. The braincase is more elongated. At Omo in Ethiopia, the dated ash lies above the fossil, so the fossil is at least that old. Ask what was dated, and where it lay.

scenes.visual: Left: Jebel Irhoud skull with face highlighted as modern and braincase outlined as elongated, burnt flints beside it. Right: sediment cross-section with skull in a middle band and a pale ash layer above, an arrow labeled "at least" pointing down from the ash.

scenes.tts: How do we know about the meetings? Sampled genomes with ancestry outside Africa share more variants with Neanderthal D N A than sampled African genomes do. A test called the D statistic measures that surplus. It is not a percentage of ancestry. On its own it is a clue, not proof, because old structure inside Africa could also produce it. Stronger evidence comes from time.

scenes.visual: Three genome bars (sampled African, sampled Eurasian, Neanderthal); match marks pile up between Eurasian and Neanderthal; a small label "D" with a gauge tipping positive; a side note "not % ancestry"; a faint second panel of a subdivided ancestral population with a question mark, then an arrow to a clock.

scenes.tts: Every generation, recombination cuts D N A from another population into shorter pieces. Ust Ishim was a man in western Siberia who lived about forty-five thousand years ago. His Neanderthal segments were longer than ours. From their length, researchers inferred gene flow seven to thirteen thousand years before he lived. At Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, three people had Neanderthal ancestors only a few generations back.

scenes.visual: A chromosome bar with one long Neanderthal block; generation ticks cut it into shorter pieces. Then two bars side by side: Ust'-Ishim (about 45,000 years) with long blocks, present-day with short ones; a bracket of 7,000 to 13,000 years before him on a timeline. Brief inset: Bacho Kiro with three figures and very long blocks.

scenes.tts: Denisovans are known mostly from D N A, such as a finger bone in Denisova Cave in Siberia. Another fragment from that cave, Denisova eleven, came from a child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. At sites where the two genomes differ, it carried one version of each. Archaic groups mixed with each other, too.

scenes.tts: Some of that inherited D N A still matters. Researchers inferred that sampled Melanesians carry about four to six percent Denisovan ancestry. In Tibetans, a version of E-pass one, a gene in the low-oxygen response, probably came from Denisovans or a related group, and rose because it helped at high altitude. That is adaptive introgression. All people alive today are one species. Most common variants are shared worldwide, and genetic variation does not divide people into discrete races.
